summary.text: Reducing the coefficient modulo \(2\), the signs disappear and Kummer’s parity criterion characterizes the contributing triples \((n,k,j)\) by carry-free binary conditions. The involution \((n,k,j)\mapsto(k+j,k,n-k)\) cancels all nonfixed contributions, while its fixed-point conditions force \(j=0\) and \(k=n\), hence \(m=n(n+1)\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{r\ge 0}x^r\frac{(1+x^r)^r}{(1+x^{r+1})^{r+1}}
   =\sum_{m\ge 0}a(m)x^m.
\]
We prove that if \(a(m)\) is odd, then \(m=n(n+1)\) for some nonnegative integer \(n\).

We begin by writing the coefficients explicitly. For each fixed \(r\), the ordinary binomial theorem and the negative binomial expansion give
\[
(1+x^r)^r=\sum_{k=0}^r\binom{r}{k}x^{rk}
\]
and
\[
(1+x^{r+1})^{-(r+1)}
 =\sum_{j\ge 0}(-1)^j\binom{r+j}{j}x^{(r+1)j}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
x^r\frac{(1+x^r)^r}{(1+x^{r+1})^{r+1}}
 =\sum_{k=0}^r\sum_{j\ge0}
 (-1)^j\binom{r}{k}\binom{r+j}{j}
 x^{r(k+1)+(r+1)j}.
\]
Thus, for every \(m\),
\[
a(m)=
\sum_{\substack{r,k,j\ge0\\ k\le r\\
 m=r(k+1)+(r+1)j}}
(-1)^j\binom{r}{k}\binom{r+j}{j}.
\tag{1}
\]
This is a finite sum: the displayed equation implies \(r\le m\), \(k\le r\le m\), and \(j\le m\).

We will use the following standard parity criterion for binomial coefficients. Write \(u\mathbin{\&}v\) for the bitwise AND of two nonnegative integers.

**Binary binomial parity lemma.** For all \(u,v\ge0\),
\[
\binom{u+v}{u}\text{ is odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u\mathbin{\&}v=0.
\tag{2}
\]
Equivalently, the binomial coefficient is odd exactly when the binary addition of \(u\) and \(v\) involves no carries.

For completeness, this follows directly from the binomial theorem over the field with two elements. If \(N=\sum_i\epsilon_i2^i\) is the binary expansion of \(N\), then in characteristic two,
\[
(1+X)^N
 =\prod_{i:\epsilon_i=1}(1+X)^{2^i}
 =\prod_{i:\epsilon_i=1}(1+X^{2^i}).
\]
Hence the coefficient \(\binom NK\) is odd precisely when every binary digit occurring in \(K\) also occurs in \(N\). Applied with \(N=u+v\) and \(K=u\), this says exactly that adding \(u\) and \(v\) has no carry. A carry occurs in that addition precisely when \(u\) and \(v\) have an overlapping binary \(1\)-digit, which is equivalent to \(u\mathbin{\&}v\ne0\). This proves (2).

Reduce (1) modulo \(2\). The sign \((-1)^j\) becomes \(1\), and a summand is nonzero modulo \(2\) exactly when both of its binomial factors are odd. Define \(S_m\) to be the finite set of triples \((r,k,j)\) of nonnegative integers satisfying
\[
k\le r,
\qquad
m=r(k+1)+(r+1)j,
\tag{3}
\]
and
\[
\binom rk\text{ is odd},

dqquad
\binom{r+j}{j}\text{ is odd}.
\tag{4}
\]
Then (1) gives
\[
a(m)\equiv |S_m|\pmod 2.
\tag{5}
\]
We shall construct an involution on \(S_m\) and identify all its fixed points.

Take \((r,k,j)\in S_m\), and put
\[
d=r-k.
\]
Thus \(r=k+d\). By (2), the oddness of \(\binom rk=\binom{k+d}{k}\) is equivalent to
\[
k\mathbin{\&}d=0.
\tag{6}
\]
Similarly, the oddness of \(\binom{r+j}{j}=\binom{j+r}{j}\) is equivalent to
\[
j\mathbin{\&}r=0.
\tag{7}
\]
Condition (6) says that the binary digits of \(k\) and \(d\) are disjoint, so their sum \(r=k+d\) is obtained without carries: the set of binary \(1\)-digits of \(r\) is exactly the disjoint union of those of \(k\) and \(d\). Condition (7) therefore implies that \(j\) is bitwise disjoint from both \(k\) and \(d\). In particular,
\[
k\mathbin{\&}j=0,
\qquad
d\mathbin{\&}j=0.
\tag{8}
\]
Combining (6) and (8), \(d\) is bitwise disjoint from \(k+j\): indeed \(k\) and \(j\) are themselves disjoint, and neither has a binary \(1\)-digit in common with \(d\). Hence
\[
d\mathbin{\&}(k+j)=0.
\tag{9}
\]
We will also need the observation that every binary \(1\)-digit of \(d\) occurs in \(r=k+d\). Thus
\[
d\mathbin{\&}r=d.
\tag{10}
\]

Now define
\[
T(r,k,j)=(k+j,\ k,\ r-k)=(k+j,k,d).
\tag{11}
\]
We verify that this is again an element of \(S_m\). First, its second coordinate is at most its first, since \(k\le k+j\). Next, the exponent equation is preserved. Using \(r=k+d\), the original right-hand side in (3) is
\[
(k+d)(k+1)+(k+d+1)j,
\]
whereas the right-hand side corresponding to the transformed triple is
\[
(k+j)(k+1)+(k+j+1)d.
\]
Expanding both expressions shows they are equal:
\[
(k+d)(k+1)+(k+d+1)j
=(k+j)(k+1)+(k+j+1)d.
\tag{12}
\]
Thus the transformed triple also represents the same exponent \(m\).

It remains to check the two parity conditions. For the transformed triple, the first binomial coefficient is
\[
\binom{k+j}{k},
\]
which is odd by (2) and \(k\mathbin{\&}j=0\). The second one is
\[
\binom{(k+j)+d}{d},
\]
which is odd by (2) and (9). Therefore \(T\) maps \(S_m\) into itself.

Moreover, \(T\) is an involution. Indeed, after the first application the new first coordinate is \(k+j\), the new second coordinate is \(k\), and their difference is \(j\). The third coordinate is \(d=r-k\). Applying the same rule again gives
\[
T(k+j,k,d)=(k+d,k,(k+j)-k)=(r,k,j).
\tag{13}
\]
Thus every non-fixed orbit of \(T\) consists of exactly two elements.

We now analyze the fixed points. Suppose that \((r,k,j)\in S_m\) is fixed by \(T\). Comparing first coordinates in (11) gives
\[
k+j=r.
\tag{14}
\]
Since \(d=r-k\), this is equivalent to
\[
j=d.
\tag{15}
\]
But (10) says \(d\mathbin{\&}r=d\), while (7), together with \(j=d\), says
\[
d\mathbin{\&}r=0.
\]
Therefore \(d=0\). It follows from (15) that \(j=0\), and from \(d=r-k=0\) that \(k=r\). Substituting these values into the exponent equation (3), we obtain
\[
m=r(r+1)+(r+1)\cdot0=r(r+1).
\tag{16}
\]
Thus every fixed point of the involution yields the required pronic form for \(m\).

Finally, suppose \(a(m)\) is odd. By (5), the finite set \(S_m\) has odd cardinality. An involution on a finite set partitions the set into two-element orbits together with its fixed points. Since the two-element orbits contribute an even number of elements, an involution on a set of odd cardinality must have at least one fixed point. Applying the fixed-point analysis above to such a fixed point gives a nonnegative integer \(r\) with
\[
m=r(r+1).
\]
This proves that an odd term can occur only at an index of the form \(n(n+1)\).
